evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Recent work identified a neural signature of confidence occurring prior to both the choice and confidence report.
source: Some recent work identified a neural signature of confidence occurring prior to both the choice and confidence report (Gherman and Philiastides, 2015, Gherman and Philiastides, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Pre-choice neural signals that dissociate high from low confidence do not imply pre-choice awareness.
source: However, findings such as these should be interpreted with caution, because pre-choice neural signals that dissociate high from low confidence do not imply pre-choice awareness.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of neural signals.

claim: Errors can be reliably predicted from alpha band activity tens of seconds before the decision actually takes place.
source: For example, it is known that errors can be reliably predicted from alpha band activity tens of seconds before the decision actually takes place (O'Connell et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Recent advances in finger tracking might allow new light to be cast on whether metacognitive experiences such as error awareness and confidence can emerge prior to choice commitment.
source: Recent advances in finger tracking might allow new light to be cast on the question of whether metacognitive experiences such as error awareness and confidence can emerge prior to choice commitment (Dotan et al., 2018; Dotan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research possibilities, with citations to relevant methodological studies.

claim: Vanilla evidence accumulation models fail to reproduce certain behavioral effects, such as the effects of fine-grained manipulations of speed/accuracy trade-off on the precise shapes of correct and error RT distributions.
source: A common criticism of 'vanilla' evidence accumulation models (the DDM being the most popular example) is that they fail to reproduce certain behavioral effects – for example, the effects of fine-grained manipulations of speed/accuracy trade-off on the precise shapes of correct and error RT distributions (Rafiei and Rahnev, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Certain classes of evidence accumulation model like the DDM lack biological plausibility, and alternative formulations prescribing a race between distinct accumulators are better candidates for realization in neural circuits.
source: Another criticism is that certain classes of evidence accumulation model (e.g. those like the DDM that prescribe the diffusion of a single, one-dimensional decision variable) lack biological plausibility, and that alternative formulations (e.g. those prescribing a race between two or more distinct accumulators) are better candidates for realization in neural circuits.
evidence: This describes a criticism of certain models based on considerations of biological plausibility.

claim: Augmenting evidence accumulation models with additional features has allowed these models to capture previously problematic features of behavioral data.
source: However, we note in response that augmenting evidence accumulation models with additional features (ideally those supported by neurophysiological findings) has in several cases allowed these models to capture previously problematic features of behavioral data – one example being evidence-independent urgency signals in the case of the speed/accuracy trade-off (Hanks et al., 2014; Murphy et al., 2016; Steinemann et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: One-dimensional diffusion processes like those prescribed by the DDM can be recast as competitive interactions between discrete accumulators.
source: Moreover, one-dimensional diffusion processes like those prescribed by the DDM can be recast as competitive interactions between discrete accumulators (Bogacz et al., 2006; Usher and McClelland, 2001) which in turn can be well approximated by biologically plausible cortical circuit models (Murphy et al., 2021; Wang, 2002; Wimmer et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Evidence accumulation is the dominant algorithmic account of how decisions are formed.
source: On current balance, we view evidence accumulation as the dominant algorithmic account of how decisions are formed, which in turn provides a solid foundation for the proposal that post-decisional accumulation is responsible for the various aspects of performance monitoring that have been the focus here'.
evidence: This is an evaluative statement about the status of evidence accumulation models based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Some doubt has been cast on whether a selective metacognitive decision variable is actually represented in the brain.
source: First, some doubt has been cast on whether a selective metacognitive DV is actually represented in the brain.
evidence: This is a statement about ongoing debate in the field.

claim: It has been argued that decision confidence can be explained without resorting to metacognitive representations.
source: For example, it has been argued that decision confidence can be explained without resorting to 'metacognitive' representations (Kepecs et al., 2008; Kiani and Shadlen, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: It should not be taken for granted that an ERP will provide a pure readout of a decision variable.
source: Second, even if such a DV is used by the brain, it should not be taken for granted that an ERP will provide a pure readout of it.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement based on knowledge about ERP signals.

claim: ERPs can reflect the superimposition of different neurocognitive processes.
source: It is well understood that ERPs can reflect the superimposition of different neurocognitive processes (Luck, 2014), and it is therefore possible that the Pe should not be interpreted in as straightforward a fashion as our proposal suggests.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a methodological reference.

claim: It is imperative to design experimental paradigms that minimize the possibility of mixing of the Pe with other signals and coincident cognitive processes.
source: In this regard, it is imperative to design experimental paradigms that minimize the possibility of mixing of the Pe with other signals and coincident cognitive processes, an approach that was also central to recent studies identifying the CPP with perceptual decision formation (O'Connell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation with a citation to a relevant study.

claim: It will be informative to examine whether manipulations that selectively influence post-decisional evidence accumulation affect the Pe component in specific ways predicted by the proposed account.
source: It will also be highly informative to build on the work reviewed above (Steinhauser and Yeung, 2010, Steinhauser and Yeung, 2012) to further examine whether manipulations that selectively influence post-decisional evidence accumulation affect the Pe component in specific ways predicted by our account.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions with citations to relevant studies.

claim: Neural signals of performance monitoring can be understood within the context of post-decisional evidence accumulation.
source: In the current review, we have discussed the idea that neural signals of performance monitoring can be understood within the context of post-decisional evidence accumulation.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main proposal of the review.

claim: Post-decisional evidence accumulation can explain how error detection and decision confidence arise from the same algorithmic process and relate to adaptive behavior.
source: Such an account can explain how error detection and decision confidence arise from the same algorithmic process and relate to adaptive behavior.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the explanatory power of the proposed framework.

claim: The proposed framework opens up exciting avenues of research concerning the neural origin of post-decisional performance monitoring signals and how these signals integrate different sources of evidence for an error.
source: Moreover, it opens up exciting avenues of research concerning the neural origin of post-decisional performance monitoring signals and how these neural signals integrate different sources of evidence for an error.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions arising from the proposed framework.

claim: Figure 1B shows that the Pe gradually ramps up preceding the detection of errors, whereas it is diminished in amplitude or even absent for undetected errors.
source: Consistent with this, the Pe gradually ramps up preceding the detection of errors, whereas it is diminished in amplitude or even absent for undetected errors (right panel). (B) Reproduced from Figure 2 Murphy et al., 2015.
evidence: This describes data shown in Figure 1B, which is reproduced from a cited study.

claim: Figure 1C shows that Pe amplitude scales inversely with reported level of confidence.
source: Consistent with this, Pe amplitude has been shown to scale inversely with reported level of confidence (right panel). (C) Reproduced from Figure 3 Boldt and Yeung, 2015.
evidence: This describes data shown in Figure 1C, which is reproduced from a cited study.

claim: Figure 1D shows that the Pe positively predicts the height of the decision boundary on the following trial.
source: Consistent with this, the Pe positively predicts the height of the decision boundary on the following trial (right panel). (D) Replotted from Figure 8 Desender et al., 2019a.
evidence: This describes data shown in Figure 1D, which is replotted from a cited study.
